title: Why do odd numbers always add up to squares?
description: A picture of a square grid shows why the odd numbers add up to squares, and why a bigger L shape around any square keeps the pattern going forever. Keeko's doubt, that a picture explains only the size that is drawn, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: the L shape around any square has one more than two times its side, which is the next odd number, so the pattern goes on forever. Watch for students who think a picture proves only the size drawn.

source: Why does this happen? Do you think it will happen forever?
video_script.why: The child sees why the totals are squares and why the pattern goes on forever, because the L shape around any square holds the next odd number of dots.
video_script.substitution: The L shape around a square of side n holds n + n + 1 dots, which is the next odd number.
video_script.anchor: a six by six square of dots with an L shape of thirteen dots waiting around its top and right sides
video_script.wrong_answer: a picture explains only the size that is drawn
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a picture explains only the size that is drawn, so the pattern may stop. The L shape around any square has one row, one column and one corner dot, so the same steps work for every size, and the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, it happens forever, for a square grid of any size

final_answer.value: Yes, it happens forever. The reason: a square grid of any size can be cut into nested L-shapes with 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots.
final_answer.spoken: yes, it happens forever, for a square grid of any size

hold_back: Yes, it happens forever, for a square grid of any size
never_show: a picture explains only the size that is drawn
maths_rules: an L shape around a 6 by 6 square has 6 + 6 + 1 = 13 dots
an L shape around an n by n square has n + n + 1 dots, the next odd number
check: an L shape around a 4 by 4 square has 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 dots, and 16 + 9 = 25 = 5 x 5
slip: the same steps work for a square of every size
video_script.design: One idea: the L shape around any square is the next odd number, so the pattern never stops. Assumes nested L shapes of one, three, five. Wrong idea: a picture proves only the size drawn. The grid stays on the board to the end.
